newsitem.title: UK: East European private investment faces hurdles.
newsitem.headline: East European private investment faces hurdles.

text.p: Private equity fund investment in central and eastern Europe has grown sharply since mid-1995 but still face barriers, bankers said on Tuesday.

Total committed investment in equity funds in central and eastern Europe at the end of 1996 stood at $13.6 billion, of which $6.26 billion was in private funds, according to European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) data.

"There has been an influx but if you look at it from a global standpoint, it is still a very small amount of money that is coming from the foreign investor to central and Eastern Europe," David Hartford, executive vice president of Pioneer Investment Poland, told an EBRD seminar.

The growth in investment by funds contrasts with a 25 percent fall in total foreign direct investment in central and eastern Europe, excluding the Commonwealth of Independent States, to $7.13 billion in 1996 from $9.52 billion in 1995.
The EBRD says this was due to large-scale privatisation in the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland in 1995.

EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere said the whole region was underperforming in this respect, noting that Singapore last year attracted about half as much foreign direct investment as eastern Europe, although its population is just three million.
But Hartford said the role of venture capital was not fully understood in the region.

"Private equity not being understood is endemic. There is no question that the participation of venture capital in the process of building companies is not well understood in central Europe," he said.

A two-year study by the European Venture Capital Association showed the funds encountered challenges in investing because of factors including poorly developed capital markets and a lack of entrepreneurial culture.
Legislation and tax regimes often made it difficult to set up funds and local institutions were not always permitted to invest, Hartford said.
However, there were differences across the region. "Obviously the situation in Poland is different from that in Bulgaria," he added.

Kurt Geiger, co-head of the EBRD's financial institutions team, said private equity funds had a key role in economies in transition which generally lacked the local savers and investors who bought into funds in developed economies.
He said there had been significant growth in private direct equity investment over the past 18 months, to $6.26 billion from $3.55 billion.
The biggest growth has been in funds which are not linked to the EBRD or other international financial institutions. They accounted for 25 percent of the total.
"We would like to see this trend grow much more," he said.
The EBRD leads 19 of its own private equity funds with $632 million in equity, of which $546 million was from the bank.

Geiger said that 60 percent of the investment of the EBRD's own private equity funds went to the Visegrad countries -- Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia. Poland took the major share with 27 percent.
The Commonwealth of Independent States accounted for 26 percent, including 11 percent invested in Russia.

In future the ERBRD would focus on selective country funds of $30-50 million and on large regional funds of at least $120 million. It would also seek contributions from domestic institutions to funds.
This had already happened in Poland and a deal was close in the Czech Republic.
